title: How to Manage Up Without Sounding Like a Suck-Up
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Molteni argues that managing up works through respect and empathy, not flattery. Opening with a colleague whose loud agreement on a call fools no one, she says the real secret, learned from a respected leader, is to be easy to work with: patient, a good listener, someone people do not dread messaging. She illustrates with a case where her technical team stopped a senior leader from adopting a poorly vetted application by consolidating feedback into one explanation, waiting until he was calm, and then supplying external documentation. She then describes the shift from order-taker to trusted advisor through taking initiative and owning solutions. Her framing is that managing up is simply empathy in action. The piece is aimed at tech professionals, and its examples are workplace rather than classroom ones.
points: Flattery rarely works on reasonable leaders; being easy to work with is what earns respect in both directions.
Managing up succeeds when disagreement is packaged as a consolidated explanation, delivered after the leader has had time to absorb it.
A leader who confides in or brainstorms with you is signalling that you are already a trusted advisor regardless of title.
Initiative, such as asking about someone's discomfort or owning a fix, separates advisors from order-takers.
Managing up is empathy applied to the person above you, which turns it into an open conversation rather than a struggle.
quotes: She had a knack for relationship management and building bridges across various teams, which helped her get things done when collaboration arose.
This simple skill of being easy to work with is not limited to the tech world. It is applicable across most industries.
Have you ever dreaded sending that email or Slack message to someone because you felt like you were on eggshells? Is that respect, or fear?
As Travis Bradberry and Jean Greaves explain in "Emotional Intelligence 2.0", you have to "Explain "our decisions, not just make them
This is a good sign if your manager or another leader is brainstorming or confiding with you. It means you are most likely a trusted advisor, regardless of your title.
If you sit there and just wait for orders or direct instructions like you are reading a Lego kit assembly model, you will not become a trusted advisor.
You are trusted because you innovate and change even when you are not directly prompted. You do not rest on your laurels, so to speak.
